value.label: Router (computing)
value.definition: A networking device that forwards packets between networks using Layer-3 addressing and routing/forwarding information.

value.name: Router versus switch
value.router: Uses Layer-3 destination IP/prefix to forward between IP networks
value.switch: Uses Layer-2 MAC addresses to bridge frames
value.overlap: Multilayer switches can also perform Layer-3 routing

value.distinction: Routing computes/maintains route choices; forwarding applies a selected FIB entry to a packet.
Routing table holds route information; FIB is a forwarding-optimized structure derived from it.
Router primarily uses Layer-3 destination IP; switch bridges using Layer-2 MAC addresses.
Multilayer switches can route between subnets, so capabilities overlap.
Basic forwarding does not guarantee delivery; endpoints provide reliability where needed.
NAT maps addressing/connection information; the source says it is not universally regarded as a security feature.
Control plane computes route state/FIB; forwarding plane applies FIB to packets.
Static route is manually configured; dynamic route is learned through a protocol.
Default route is used when no more-specific destination entry matches.
Access serves customer/site connectivity; distribution aggregates traffic and may enforce WAN QoS.
Distribution aggregates/policies traffic; core provides high-bandwidth backbone transit.
Edge peers at network boundaries; core carries traffic between edge routers within an AS.
P is provider transit; PE connects CE and provides VPN services.
PE is provider-side; CE is customer-side edge.
Tail drop waits for a full buffer; RED/WRED can drop earlier, with WRED differentiating traffic types.
ASIC accelerates common operations; CPU handles packets/functions requiring special attention.
Wi-Fi router integrates routing, switching, and AP; a residential gateway may also integrate a modem.
Interfaces, processors, buffers, and accelerators execute work; OS/routing code supplies behavior/configuration.
Basic IP forwarding uses header addressing and usually not payload.
AS is a routing/policy domain; physical interfaces/links are the transmission substrate.

value.misconception: A router guarantees packets reach the final destination.
value.correction: A router forwards hop by hop; basic connectionless routing does not guarantee delivery.

value.misconception: Routing and forwarding are the same operation.
value.correction: Routing maintains/selects routes and builds the FIB; forwarding uses the FIB for each packet.

value.misconception: A router normally chooses routes by reading the application payload.
value.correction: Pure IP forwarding primarily uses destination IP and optional header hints, not payload.

value.misconception: The routing table and FIB are identical.
value.correction: The FIB is derived from route information and optimized for forwarding.

value.misconception: NAT is a complete security control.
value.correction: NAT is not universally recognized as a security feature; firewalling and policy are distinct.

value.misconception: All routers are ASIC appliances.
value.correction: Routers range from software/CPU systems to network processors and ASIC-assisted devices.

value.misconception: Every router needs separate Wi-Fi AP and switch hardware.
value.correction: Home Wi-Fi routers commonly integrate router, switch, and AP functions, sometimes with modem.

value.misconception: The default route is the only route in a router.
value.correction: Route tables can contain specific static/dynamic routes and a default route for unmatched destinations.

value.misconception: A router and Layer-3 switch are wholly separate capabilities.
value.correction: Multilayer switches can route between subnets.

value.misconception: More buffering removes congestion.
value.correction: Buffers are finite; queues can increase latency and queue-management policies may drop packets.

value.misconception: QoS creates additional bandwidth.
value.correction: QoS prioritizes traffic but does not create capacity.

value.misconception: The Internet has one centrally controlled router backbone.
value.correction: Major ISP systems collectively form a distributed backbone core; there is no single central backbone router.

value.misconception: Open-source router software is automatically more secure.
value.correction: The article reports a debated argument about visibility of flaws, not a universal proof.

value.misconception: Control plane and forwarding plane must be separate physical boxes.
value.correction: The article describes functional units operating simultaneously; physical separation is not required by that statement.

value.misconception: A route entry guarantees end-to-end reachability.
value.correction: A route informs a local forwarding decision; downstream failures and congestion can still interrupt delivery.

source_claims.claim: A router forwards packets between computer networks using network-layer destination information and routing information/policy.
A router is a Layer-3 device because its primary forwarding decision is based on the destination IP address.
The control plane maintains routing information and builds a FIB; the forwarding plane consults the FIB to forward packets.
Routing tables may include static, dynamic, and default routes; a default route may also be obtained by DHCP.
Connectionless router/gateway design does not assure reliable delivery; reliability is left to hosts.
Tail drop, RED, and WRED are queue-management policies used when packets arrive faster than a router can process/transmit them.
QoS classifies traffic and affects processing priority; it is important for latency-sensitive VoIP traffic.
Router implementations range from CPU/software forwarding to network processors and ASIC-accelerated hardware.
Router roles include access, distribution, core, edge, provider, provider-edge, customer-edge, interior, exterior, and border/gateway.
Routers may integrate firewall, VPN, and NAT features, but NAT is not universally recognized as a security feature.
Wi-Fi routers combine router, switch, and wireless access point functions, and residential gateways may also integrate a modem.
The article traces router precursors from NPL/ARPANET interface computers to CYCLADES, Xerox PARC, DARPA, BBN, and 1981 multiprotocol router programs.
Routers running multiple routing protocols may selectively redistribute routes between them.
Pure IP forwarding usually uses Layer-3 addresses and optional header hints, not payload inspection.
The source does not deeply specify ASIC microarchitecture, MTU/fragmentation mechanics, or specific routing algorithms.

fields.label: Overview
fields.value: A relationship-rich semantic graph of network routing: path selection, routing algorithms, delivery schemes, protocol families, metrics, multi-agent policies, congestion, hardware/software implementation, history, and route analytics.

value.name: Routing versus forwarding
steps: select route according to protocol and policy
match each packet destination against FIB
conditions: routing is control/path selection; forwarding is per-packet transit

value.name: Distance-vector update
steps: advertise known destination costs to neighbors
compare received estimates with current estimates
install improved cost and next hop
conditions: distributed neighbor exchange; Bellman–Ford style

value.name: Link-state shortest path
steps: derive best next hops and routing table
conditions: each router computes its own shortest-path tree

value.name: Path-vector inter-domain route
steps: select an AS-level route under policy
conditions: inter-domain; AS speakers exchange path descriptions

value.name: Route precedence
steps: compare route sources using implementation-specific preference
conditions: metric comparison across protocols is not directly meaningful; administrative distance is implementation-specific

value.name: Message delivery schemes
steps: choose a single receiver, all nodes, an interested group, or one group member
apply address and routing behavior appropriate to scheme
conditions: broadcast scope depends on network/subnet; anycast chooses one member

value.name: Queue congestion and packet drops
steps: compare arrival rate with service rate
apply tail drop, RED, or WRED when queue thresholds/capacity are reached
observe packet loss and possible flow delay
conditions: exact thresholds and policies depend on implementation/configuration

value.name: OLSR proactive neighbor discovery
conditions: mobile ad hoc networks

value.name: Hot-potato route choice
steps: choose an AS-level path under BGP policy
hand traffic to neighboring AS at that exit
compare end-to-end latency with alternative paths
conditions: local optimization can conflict with global latency optimization

value.name: Centralized WAN optimization
conditions: logically centralized control; example private data-center WANs

value.name: Distributed convergence after failure
steps: propagate updates until usable alternatives settle
conditions: convergence time and stability depend on protocol/topology

value.name: Metric-based path selection
conditions: best path depends on objective; one metric does not universally optimize all goals

value.name: Randomized intermediate routing
steps: route intermediate traffic to final destination
conditions: described as an approach to reduce congestion hot spots in some packet systems

value.name: Next-hop routing at scale
conditions: no single device needs to calculate or know the complete end-to-end path

value.name: Policy-aware route choice
conditions: commercial policy can choose a path that is not lowest-latency

value.name: Static versus dynamic routing
steps: choose manual configuration for small/stable topology or protocol learning for changing topology
update or maintain routes as conditions change
conditions: the source contrasts manually configured small networks with dynamic large networks

value.distinction: Routing selects a path/next hop; forwarding transits each packet between interfaces.
IP routing uses structured network-layer addresses; bridging is Layer-2 forwarding.
Static routes are configured manually; dynamic routes are learned/updated through protocols.
Distance vector exchanges destination costs with neighbors; link state floods topology information and computes paths locally.
Path vector advertises domain/path descriptions; distance vector advertises destination costs.
Intra-domain routing operates within an AS; inter-domain routing connects ASs.
Unicast targets one receiver; broadcast targets all nodes in scope.
Multicast targets an interested subset; broadcast targets all nodes within scope.
Anycast chooses one of several receivers sharing an address; unicast targets a specific receiver.
The routing table holds route information; the FIB is optimized for forwarding lookups.
Metrics compare routes under a protocol; administrative distance can compare sources in an implementation-specific way.
ECMP uses multiple equal-cost paths instead of only one route.
Hot-potato routing minimizes an ISP’s internal distance to exit, potentially increasing end-to-end latency.
Centralized routing can optimize global state; distributed protocols exchange local route/topology information.
Deterministic routing repeats a preferred path until information changes; randomized routing can choose an intermediate destination.
Tail drop waits for buffer exhaustion; RED begins probabilistic drops earlier.
WRED varies drop behavior by traffic type.
An AS sequence can map to multiple concrete router-level paths.
Metrics quantify path attributes; policies can override a metric-optimal path for business or administrative reasons.
Convergence is the network settling after updates; route selection chooses among candidates at a given moment.

value.misconception: Routing and forwarding are the same operation.
value.correction: Routing selects path/next-hop state; forwarding applies the FIB to individual packets.

value.misconception: Every router computes the entire end-to-end path for each packet.
value.correction: Large networks generally use next-hop routing; each node forwards toward the next hop.

value.misconception: The lowest latency route is always selected.
value.correction: Metrics and policies vary; BGP decisions may reflect business relationships or hot-potato routing.

value.misconception: A routing metric can be compared directly across all protocols.
value.correction: The source says metrics cannot be compared across routes learned from different protocols; implementations may use administrative distance.

value.misconception: Multicast is the same as broadcast.
value.correction: Multicast targets an interested subset; broadcast targets all nodes within its scope.

value.misconception: Anycast delivers to every node sharing an address.
value.correction: Anycast selects one member of the group, usually based on routing distance/cost.

value.misconception: Static routing is suitable for any rapidly changing large topology.
value.correction: The source notes manual table construction becomes infeasible for large, rapidly changing networks.

value.misconception: Link-state routing simply shares a single final route.
value.correction: Nodes flood link-state information, construct topology maps, and independently compute shortest-path trees.

value.misconception: Path-vector routing advertises only a scalar distance.
value.correction: Path-vector announcements include destination reachability and path/domain descriptions.

value.misconception: Adding a network link always improves every user’s route.
value.correction: Under selfish multi-agent route choices, Braess’s paradox shows an added road can increase travel time.

value.misconception: A full buffer is the only way to manage congestion.
value.correction: The source describes RED/WRED early drop behavior in addition to tail drop.

value.misconception: A shortest AS-level path uniquely determines the router-level path.
value.correction: Multiple router-level paths may correspond to a selected AS-level path.

value.misconception: Centralized routing is limited to a single small network.
value.correction: The source describes centralized optimization across geographically distributed private data-center WANs.

value.misconception: Dynamic routing prevents all routing failures.
value.correction: Dynamic routing adapts to failures, but incorrect routing, flapping, degradation, and downtime remain possible.

value.misconception: A router must inspect application payloads to choose an IP route.
value.correction: Pure IP forwarding typically uses Layer-3 addresses and optional header hints, not packet payload content.

source_claims.claim: Routing selects a path; forwarding moves packets between interfaces.
Routing decisions usually rely on routing tables populated manually or with protocol assistance.
Structured IP addresses allow route aggregation and scale better than unstructured bridging in large networks.
Unicast, broadcast, multicast, and anycast represent distinct delivery semantics.
Dynamic routing updates route tables using protocol information and dominates the Internet.
Distance-vector routing uses Bellman–Ford-style iterative neighbor cost exchange.
Link-state routers flood topology information and independently calculate least-cost paths.
OLSR uses Hello, TC, and multipoint relay mechanisms for proactive ad hoc routing.
Path-vector routing advertises path/domain descriptions for inter-domain reachability.

Inter-AS route choices can reflect commercial relationships and hot-potato policies rather than global latency.
Centralized routing can optimize network-wide performance objectives in private WANs.
Incorrect routing and route flapping can cause performance degradation or downtime.
Early router concepts emerged from NPL, ARPANET, CYCLADES, Xerox PARC, and DARPA-related work.

source_claims.summary: DHH extracted Rails from Basecamp at 37signals and released it open source in July 2004.

source_claims.title: Rails 2.3
source_claims.summary: Templates, Engines, Rack and Metal expanded Rails extensibility and optimized routing.

source_claims.title: Merb
source_claims.summary: Rails and Merb collaborated and Merb merged into Rails 3.

source_claims.title: Rails evolution
source_claims.summary: Rails 3.1 through 8.1 progressively changed JS, jobs, storage, database, deployment, code loading and self-hosting.

source_claims.title: MVC mechanics
source_claims.summary: Models map to tables/files, controllers handle requests/actions, routes map requests to actions, and views render HTML.

source_claims.title: Deployment
source_claims.summary: Rails commonly sits behind Apache/Nginx/Passenger and uses MySQL or PostgreSQL.

source_claims.title: Philosophy
source_claims.summary: CoC, DRY, fat models/skinny controllers, Rails Doctrine, conceptual compression and robust security shape Rails design.

source_claims.title: Scalability
source_claims.summary: Source documents historical Rails scaling criticism and emphasizes architecture choices such as database, cache and servers.

source_claims.title: Security
source_claims.summary: Source documents mass assignment, CookieStore persistence and Space analysis findings.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Ruby is the language; Rails is the framework written in Ruby.
MVC model is architectural role; Active Record supplies ORM behavior.
Controller is component; action is a response unit within controller.
Route maps an external request to an action; action does not itself define public reachability.
ERB is a template engine; Rails is the application framework.
Rails is framework; Rack is web-server interface.
Rails commonly sits behind a front-end server rather than directly on Internet.
Hotwire is client/web interaction family integrated as Rails 7 default.
Turbo replaced Turbolinks in Rails 7.
Older Rails plugins were deprecated in favor of standard gems.
Scaling depends on broader system architecture, not only framework.
Framework security mechanisms coexist with application/configuration vulnerabilities.

misconceptions.correction: Rails is a Ruby framework.

misconceptions.claim: Every Rails request is directly handled by Rails from the Internet
misconceptions.correction: Rails commonly sits behind a front-end web server.

misconceptions.claim: MVC model is identical to Active Record
misconceptions.correction: Active Record is the ORM implementation used for model/database behavior.

misconceptions.claim: A controller action is automatically public
misconceptions.correction: A route must map an external request to the controller action.

misconceptions.claim: Rails scaling is only a framework problem
misconceptions.correction: Source emphasizes database, cache, server and architecture choices.
Rails 7 made import maps the default and moved away from Webpack as default.
Rails 7 replaced Turbolinks with Turbo + Stimulus.

misconceptions.claim: Rails extensions are primarily custom plugins
misconceptions.correction: Rails 3.2 deprecated custom plugin framework in favor of gems.

misconceptions.claim: Ruby and Rails are interchangeable names
misconceptions.correction: Ruby is the language; Rails is written in Ruby.
Source documents encryption, CSP, security work and security vulnerabilities.
